note: Two instantiations per unit, one in baking and one in carpentry. copied_runs counts consecutive words, function words included, against the whole paper.

instantiations: Home cooks want a loaf that keeps for a week. However, a cold kitchen slows the rise, and guessing the time fails. A timed rest gives a loaf that holds, by letting the dough finish its own work.
Woodworkers want a frame that stays square. However, green timber twists as it dries, and guessing the cut fails. A dry-fit gives a frame that holds, by letting the joint seat on its own.
We built step one, a long rest, and step two, a hot bake. The two depend on each other and together make the loaf plan, meant to help a cook feed a family on a weekday.
We built step one, a dry-fit, and step two, a glue-up. The two depend on each other and together make the frame plan, meant to help a maker finish a shelf for a client.

For step one, we use a fold-and-rest method to improve a plain mix. The dough takes a handful of folds and gives two rises. The short rise covers the morning and the long one the afternoon. We baked it, and the spring cleared the mark we set, and the crumb came out even.

For step one, we use a scribe-and-fit method to improve a plain butt joint. The piece takes a handful of passes and gives two fits. The short fit covers the rail and the long one the stile. We tested it, and the hold cleared the mark we set, and the faces came out flush.

For step two, the idea is to follow a "rest, then bake" plan. It runs in four beats. Leave the dough alone for the first while; bake it once it springs and clears the line. The lines are one finger and two fingers for the wheat, and a knuckle and a thumb for the rye.

For step two, the idea is to follow a "fit, then glue" plan. It runs in four beats. Leave the joint alone for the first while; glue it once it seats and clears the line. The lines are one hair and two hairs for the oak, and a shaving and a curl for the pine.
We use the poke test to read how lively the dough is and use it to decide how long to bake.
We use the flex test to read how stiff the board is and use it to decide how deep to cut.

We can say the following after the bake, the taste test, and the keeping test. The slow proof handled the first loaf. The dough started small, and after the afternoon it filled the tin. For the second loaf, the proof it was the right one is that the salt was tuned; the crumb also beat a plain mix, a fast proof, and a cold proof. For the third loaf, we find the bake leans on the oven more than the salt.

We can say the following after the glue-up, the load test, and the season test. The slow clamp handled the first frame. The joint started loose, and after the afternoon it locked tight. For the second frame, the proof it was the right one is that the fit was tuned; the hold also beat a plain butt, a fast glue, and a cold glue. For the third frame, we find the build leans on the clamp more than the glue.
The proof that the recipe is the one to keep is that the salt was tuned; the rise also beats a plain mix, a fast proof, and a cold proof.
The proof that the joint is the one to keep is that the fit was tuned; the hold also beats a plain butt, a fast glue, and a cold glue.
Finally, we wrote a note for the client covering the recipe, the bake, and the taste. Moreover, how the loaf keeps is looked at.
Finally, we wrote a note for the client covering the joint, the glue-up, and the fit. Moreover, how the frame holds is looked at.

"A good loaf starts with the hands." As baking spread, home ovens became common. Yeast baking began in the 1800s. Named methods pushed it along. Although bad flour and failed batches still happen, home baking is still worth doing. After all, one bakery turns out hundreds of loaves a day.

"A good joint starts with the hands." As woodworking spread, home shops became common. Dovetail work began in the 1700s. Named methods pushed it along. Although bad timber and failed joints still happen, hand work is still worth doing. After all, one shop turns out dozens of frames a week.
Compared with mixing by feel, weighing the flour and timing the folds lets a cook get an even crumb while keeping the loaf tall.
Compared with cutting by eye, scribing the line and checking the square lets a maker get a tight joint while keeping the frame light.
From a close look at the kitchen, together with the limits the client set, the plan can be written out as follows.
From a close look at the shop, together with the limits the client set, the plan can be written out as follows.

Bake the loaf from the dough already on the bench, and give the family a warm slice. Note that the bake may use only flour milled on or before that morning. That is, we may not reach for flour that arrives later.

Build the frame from the timber already in the rack, and give the client a finished shelf. Note that the build may use only boards milled on or before that morning. That is, we may not reach for boards that arrive later.
Starting on the first Monday, the cook used one bag of flour to fill the tins from the recipe and count the loaves left after the week.
Starting on the first Monday, the maker used one stack of boards to fill the order from the cutting list and count the pieces left after the week.
Show that the amounts in the recipe are the best ones, and that the bake is the best the recipe can give. Prove that this loaf keeps longer than the others.
Show that the sizes in the cutting list are the best ones, and that the joint is the best the list can give. Prove that this frame holds more than the others.
Given the loaves above, write one or two pages for the client covering the recipe and the bake.
Given the frames above, write one or two pages for the client covering the joint and the build.
To settle on the best daily bake, the dough can be folded in stages and then joined with methods already in use to pick the loaf. The work of the bakers below gives a place to start.
To settle on the best daily build, the boards can be cut in stages and then joined with methods already in use to pick the frame. The work of the makers below gives a place to start.

Wheat dough is lively, uneven, and changes through the day. A plain count rests on an even rise, which misses the peaks. Two bakers in one year used a fold count to get a close result. Two more in the same year used a timed rest, which came out closer still. Lately the cold proof has drawn notice. One baker last year tried it.

Oak boards are lively, uneven, and move through the season. A plain measure rests on an even board, which misses the twist. Two makers in one year used a scribe to get a close fit. Two more in the same year used a dry-fit, which came out closer still. Lately the slow glue has drawn notice. One maker last year tried it.

One baker found the rye rises fast, and another shows the wheat keeps longer. A group of bakers stuck with the plain count. Compared with a plain count, a fold method catches the lively rye better. One baker set the fold method against the plain count and found the fold won. Another went further, set three methods side by side, and settled on the fold.

One maker found the pine moves fast, and another shows the oak holds longer. A group of makers stuck with the plain measure. Compared with a plain measure, a scribe catches the lively pine better. One maker set the scribe against the plain measure and found the scribe won. Another went further, set three methods side by side, and settled on the scribe.

A bake rests on reading the dough, which is kinder than baking blind. The methods fall into about two groups. One group is the timed rest. For instance, one baker tried it and checked it against a cold proof. The other group rests on a fold count. Two bakers studied it. They found it needs no thermometer, nor a clock, and can still give an even crumb.

A build rests on reading the timber, which is kinder than cutting blind. The methods fall into about two groups. One group is the dry-fit. For instance, one maker tried it and checked it against a glue-up. The other group rests on a scribe. Two makers studied it. They found it needs no gauge, nor a square, and can still give a tight joint.
To show the bakers' work more clearly, we draw a chart from the notes above.
To show the makers' work more clearly, we draw a chart from the notes above.
The order asks for a loaf the family will finish. Our work comes down to the following.
The job asks for a frame the client will keep. Our work comes down to the following.
From the dough on hand, the long rest is set up. Use its rise to set the bake time. The two together make the loaf plan, giving the family a warm loaf.
From the timber on hand, the dry-fit is set up. Use its fit to set the glue time. The two together make the frame plan, giving the client a square frame.
We show the recipe is the one to keep by tuning the salt and baking a comparison batch.
We show the joint is the one to keep by tuning the fit and building a comparison frame.
Change the oven heat for the wheat and the rye, and study how the heat changes the crumb and the crust.
Change the clamp time for the oak and the pine, and study how the time changes the hold and the look.
To spare a long description and show the bake plainly, the chart appears below.
To spare a long description and show the build plainly, the chart appears below.
A kitchen is full of small choices, so we set a few rules to keep the bake simple, and each rule is followed at once by the reason for it.
A shop is full of small choices, so we set a few rules to keep the build simple, and each rule is followed at once by the reason for it.
Rule one: the batch stays small enough not to warm the kitchen. Reason: a big batch would change how the next one rises.
Rule one: the glue stays light enough not to swell the joint. Reason: a heavy glue would change how the next joint seats.
Further rules are set for single steps. Those rules are stated where they are used.
Further rules are set for single cuts. Those rules are stated where they are used.
The chart shows the names this note uses. Any other name is explained the first time it comes up.
The chart shows the names this note uses. Any other name is explained the first time it comes up.

A cook picks the loaf from the crumb and the crust. To feed the family, the cook needs a read on the dough and then a bake time. So the plan has two steps: first read the dough, then set the bake, and last put a warm loaf on the table.

A maker picks the frame from the fit and the finish. To please the client, the maker needs a read on the timber and then a glue time. So the plan has two steps: first read the timber, then set the glue, and last hand over a square frame.

Because it handles uneven dough, bends easily, and shrugs off a cold kitchen, the fold method is used everywhere for bread. We look at using it here, drawing on the bakers above and on how lively the dough is.

Because it handles uneven timber, bends easily, and shrugs off a damp shop, the scribe is used everywhere for frames. We look at using it here, drawing on the makers above and on how lively the boards are.
When a plain count meets a lively dough, the loaf suffers because the rise drags. So many better methods have been put forward to speed it. They fall into two groups.
When a plain measure meets a lively board, the joint suffers because the fit drags. So many better methods have been put forward to speed it. They fall into two groups.
The first group. These suit only small, calm doughs. The second group. It uses both the rise and the spring. It is the better pick for a lively dough.
The first group. These suit only small, calm boards. The second group. It uses both the fit and the flex. It is the better pick for a lively board.
Since the dough is lively and the batch is large, the second group fits better. One baker found the fold method finishes fast. Given that, this bake uses the fold method for the wheat and the rye.
Since the board is lively and the job is large, the second group fits better. One maker found the scribe finishes fast. Given that, this build uses the scribe for the oak and the pine.
The bake has two parts: the rise going forward and the heat coming back. The dough moves one way. If it springs, the bake ends; otherwise, it goes back for another fold.
The build has two parts: the fit going forward and the check coming back. The joint moves one way. If it seats, the build ends; otherwise, it goes back for another pass.
Setting the loaf shape. That is, choose how many folds and how many tins. Usually, after many tries, the shape that gives the best crumb is kept.
Setting the frame shape. That is, choose how many cuts and how many joints. Usually, after many tries, the shape that gives the best fit is kept.
Start the salt and the yeast. Each one is usually picked at random from a small range.
Start the glue and the clamp. Each one is usually picked at random from a small range.
Keep folding until the sag drops below the line we set, the folding stops, and the bake ends.
Keep cutting until the gap drops below the line we set, the cutting stops, and the build ends.

When the plain method bakes the rye, it can overwork the dough, and the fast fold can also trap it in a poor shape. The rise is slow too. To bake the wheat and the rye better, this note uses the slow fold.

When the plain method builds the pine, it can overwork the joint, and the fast cut can also trap it in a poor shape. The fit is slow too. To build the oak and the pine better, this note uses the slow cut.

The slow fold can be seen as a mix of a gentle turn and a firm press. It acts like the gentle turn, slow but sure to finish, when the dough is far from ready. When the dough is close to ready, it becomes the firm press.

The slow cut can be seen as a mix of a light pass and a firm paring. It acts like the light pass, slow but sure to finish, when the joint is far from seated. When the joint is close to seated, it becomes the firm paring.

Since the later bake leans on a machine to do the mixing, we will not spell out the sums behind it. Still, so a reader can see how it works, and drawing on a standard kitchen guide, we give the steps below.

Since the later build leans on a jig to do the cutting, we will not spell out the sums behind it. Still, so a reader can see how it works, and drawing on a standard shop guide, we give the steps below.
A mixer setting handles the wheat and the rye. We only have to choose the amounts and judge the loaf.
A jig setting handles the oak and the pine. We only have to choose the sizes and judge the frame.

To meet the order, we make a short rise and a long rise for the wheat and the rye. Both take the same handful of folds, and the short rise for both is the next hour. Because the two grains behave differently, the long rise for the wheat is the next morning and for the rye the next afternoon.

To meet the job, we make a short fit and a long fit for the oak and the pine. Both take the same handful of passes, and the short fit for both is the next hour. Because the two woods behave differently, the long fit for the oak is the next morning and for the pine the next afternoon.

To avoid an overworked dough, the batch is split at random, in shares of most, some, and a little. For the wheat, set the folds to a few. For the rye, set the folds to a few more. Use the sag to judge the dough. When the folds hit the cap, the work stops.

To avoid an overworked joint, the stack is split at random, in shares of most, some, and a little. For the oak, set the passes to a few. For the pine, set the passes to a few more. Use the gap to judge the joint. When the passes hit the cap, the work stops.
The chart shows the spring of the practice batch, the trial batch, the held-back batch, and the whole clears the line we set. The same holds for the rye. The bake came out well.
The chart shows the fit of the practice stack, the trial stack, the held-back stack, and the whole clears the line we set. The same holds for the pine. The build came out well.

To let a reader feel how close the bake came, we set the baked loaf against the one we hoped for and drew the chart. The two curves sit almost on top of each other, proving the bake once more, which lets us go on to the next loaf.

To let a reader feel how close the build came, we set the finished frame against the one we hoped for and drew the chart. The two lines sit almost on top of each other, proving the build once more, which lets us go on to the next frame.

The rest method watches how the folds relate and is easy to explain. The machine method is like a closed box. It usually does better but can overwork the dough. However, our kitchen is different. We have only the dough in front of us. The dough alone is too little. So we build our own method rather than patch an old one.

The fit method watches how the cuts relate and is easy to explain. The jig method is like a closed box. It usually does better but can overwork the joint. However, our shop is different. We have only the boards in front of us. The boards alone are too little. So we build our own method rather than patch an old one.

The idea is to pick one way of baking and carry it out in steps. Since we can judge only the dough we have, and to avoid a plan too fussy to finish, we use the plainest "fold, then bake from the rise" way.

The idea is to pick one way of building and carry it out in steps. Since we can judge only the boards we have, and to avoid a plan too fussy to finish, we use the plainest "scribe, then glue from the fit" way.

Each morning we know how the dough looks that day, so we must fold in the latest dough when we guess the rise, which means each time we bake we must redo the rise and bake from that, so we call the plan a rolling bake.

Each morning we know how the boards look that day, so we must cut in the latest board when we guess the fit, which means each time we build we must redo the fit and build from that, so we call the plan a rolling build.
Please take the bench as holding flour, water, and salt, and its start as a full jar, an empty bowl, and an empty tin, as the order states.
Please take the bench as holding oak, pine, and glue, and its start as a full stack, an empty rack, and an empty clamp, as the job states.
The waiting step. This step gathers the dough the bake needs and makes no loaf. The bake leans on the rise. The bake begins once both grains have sat long enough.
The waiting step. This step gathers the boards the build needs and makes no frame. The build leans on the fit. The build begins once both woods have sat long enough.

At this step we must settle two things: when to bake and how large a loaf. Wheat: bake if the next hour's rise clears a finger, or the morning's rise clears two. Rye: bake if the next hour's rise clears a knuckle, or the afternoon's rise clears a thumb.

At this step we must settle two things: when to glue and how large a frame. Oak: glue if the next hour's fit clears a hair, or the morning's fit clears two. Pine: glue if the next hour's fit clears a shaving, or the afternoon's fit clears a curl.

The spring score says how much rise the dough gives for each bit of trouble. The score follows. In it, the rise takes the larger of the short rise or half the long rise, since a long rise risks more. If the score clears the line, the loaf is worth the trouble; if it falls short, it is not.

The fit score says how much hold the joint gives for each bit of trouble. The score follows. In it, the hold takes the larger of the short fit or half the long fit, since a long fit risks more. If the score clears the line, the frame is worth the trouble; if it falls short, it is not.

Two cases need a look. Bake both grains together. Split the dough by the two scores and use all of it. Bake only one grain. If its score clears the line, use all the dough on it; if not, use only its share.

Two cases need a look. Glue both woods together. Split the stack by the two scores and use all of it. Glue only one wood. If its score clears the line, use all the stack on it; if not, use only its share.
Bake when we expect the loaf to fall. The changes match the earlier step, so we skip the repeat. The tin count must be updated after the bake.
Glue when we expect the frame to loosen. The changes match the earlier step, so we skip the repeat. The clamp count must be updated after the glue.

We wrote our own steps to run the bake. Follow them with the dough we have, and this follows: if we start on Monday with one bag of flour and bake by the plan, then by Friday the bag becomes a full rack of loaves.

We wrote our own steps to run the build. Follow them with the boards we have, and this follows: if we start on Monday with one stack and build by the plan, then by Friday the stack becomes a full order of frames.
This part will show that our bake is the best one.
This part will show that our build is the best one.

For a given recipe, we get the best loaf only when each amount is the best amount. While writing the recipe, we set the salt from the flour we had and from kitchen habit. To show the amounts are the best ones, we try the nearby amounts.

For a given joint, we get the best frame only when each size is the best size. While writing the list, we set the depth from the timber we had and from shop habit. To show the sizes are the best ones, we try the nearby sizes.

From the order and the kitchen, the salt runs across a short list of amounts and the yeast across a longer one. We tune for the tallest loaf. Comparing the loaves, we settled on one salt and one yeast. That matches the amounts the recipe already used.

From the job and the shop, the depth runs across a short list of sizes and the width across a longer one. We tune for the stiffest frame. Comparing the frames, we settled on one depth and one width. That matches the sizes the list already used.

To check the bake, we chose a comparison batch. Think of a slow proof, a fast proof, and the loaves a bakery sells. We set up the batches and counted the loaves. For the plain ones, we skip the arithmetic.
To check the build, we chose a comparison run. Think of a slow glue, a fast glue, and the frames a shop sells. We set up the runs and counted the frames. For the plain ones, we skip the arithmetic.
Comparison one: on Monday, bake all the flour as wheat and leave it to the end, when the rack held a few loaves.
Comparison one: on Monday, build all the timber as oak and leave it to the end, when the order held a few frames.

Rank the bakes and make the chart. The chart teaches a few things. First, our bake came out on top and well ahead of the rest, which says it is the one to keep. Second, the slow proof came next, because the wheat rose hard all week. Third, the fast proof came last, because one reading misses too much and a rushed bake costs loaves.

Rank the builds and make the chart. The chart teaches a few things. First, our build came out on top and well ahead of the rest, which says it is the one to keep. Second, the slow glue came next, because the oak held firm all week. Third, the fast glue came last, because one reading misses too much and a rushed build costs frames.

Here the cost is mostly the fuel, because a loaf sitting in the tin costs nothing. The fuel depends on how many bakes and how hot each one runs. Picture one bake: a hotter oven costs more and leaves fewer loaves. To see how much the bake moves with the fuel, we change the heat and watch the loaves.

Here the cost is mostly the blades, because a frame sitting in the clamp costs nothing. The blades depend on how many cuts and how deep each one runs. Picture one cut: a deeper pass costs more and leaves fewer frames. To see how much the build moves with the blades, we change the depth and watch the frames.
Hold the recipe still and change only the heat, watching the loaves. With the recipe fixed, three cases matter: heat the wheat only, heat the rye only, and heat both. We drew the chart.
Hold the joint still and change only the depth, watching the frames. With the joint fixed, three cases matter: cut the oak only, cut the pine only, and cut both. We drew the chart.

From the chart: when the rye heat changes and the wheat stays put, the loaves swing hard. When the wheat heat changes and the rye stays put, the loaves barely move. For instance, even with the wheat oven pushed very hot, the rack still holds the same number. The change runs in a straight line. So the bake leans hard on the rye and hardly at all on the wheat.

From the chart: when the pine depth changes and the oak stays put, the frames swing hard. When the oak depth changes and the pine stays put, the frames barely move. For instance, even with the oak cut very deep, the order still holds the same number. The change runs in a straight line. So the build leans hard on the pine and hardly at all on the oak.

Because the fuel shapes the bake, the best recipe also changes when the heat changes. The aim is the most loaves, which means the rise must beat the fuel spent. We rewrote the rule so the short rise must clear a mark built from the heat. The long rise is less sure, so its mark sits a small step higher.

Because the blades shape the build, the best joint also changes when the depth changes. The aim is the most frames, which means the fit must beat the blades spent. We rewrote the rule so the short fit must clear a mark built from the depth. The long fit is less sure, so its mark sits a small step higher.
From the chart: the wheat stays calm. When the rye heat sits above the mark, little changes; below the mark, the bake swings hard and the rack changes sharply. So the earlier count no longer holds.
From the chart: the oak stays calm. When the pine depth sits above the mark, little changes; below the mark, the build swings hard and the order changes sharply. So the earlier count no longer holds.
After the checks above, we find both the recipe and the loaves lean hard on the rye heat and far less on the wheat heat.
After the checks above, we find both the joint and the frames lean hard on the pine depth and far less on the oak depth.
Our bake has these virtues.
Our build has these virtues.
We use the slow fold. Compared with a plain count and a fast proof, the bake rises higher and fits the tin better. At the same time, we make a short rise and a long rise for each grain.
We use the slow cut. Compared with a plain measure and a fast glue, the build fits tighter and seats better. At the same time, we make a short fit and a long fit for each wood.
When baking, using both the short rise and the long rise, the loaf is surer than using either one by itself.
When building, using both the short fit and the long fit, the frame is surer than using either one by itself.
The bake we wrote is a greedy one, and the loaf it gives may be the best nearby rather than the best anywhere.
The build we wrote is a greedy one, and the frame it gives may be the best nearby rather than the best anywhere.
The bake leans too hard on one grain. In the week's run, most loaves were rye and the wheat barely appeared. The plan shows a habit of chasing the rise, and it notices a change a little late.
The build leans too hard on one wood. In the week's run, most frames were pine and the oak barely appeared. The plan shows a habit of chasing the fit, and it notices a change a little late.
Short on time, the heart of the plan is fairly plain. Given how fussy a kitchen gets, we might later try a bake that learns from each loaf.
Short on time, the heart of the plan is fairly plain. Given how fussy a shop gets, we might later try a build that learns from each frame.
To the client. From the bake team. About the bread. Dated the Monday after delivery. Dear client, we are glad to tell you we built a bake from the dough alone and tried to give the best loaf.
To the client. From the shop team. About the frame. Dated the Monday after delivery. Dear client, we are glad to tell you we built a frame from the timber alone and tried to give the best joint.
As you asked, we built a bake that helps you choose whether to start, wait, or bake each morning.
As you asked, we built a frame that helps you choose whether to cut, wait, or glue each morning.

A sure rise is the base of a good loaf. The dough is lively and suits a fold method. The plain way uses a fast fold, which often spoils the loaf because the rise drags. So we built a slow fold. We baked it, and the spring cleared the line we set, and the crumb came out even.

A sure fit is the base of a good frame. The timber is lively and suits a scribe. The plain way uses a fast cut, which often spoils the joint because the fit drags. So we built a slow cut. We tried it, and the hold cleared the line we set, and the faces came out flush.

The idea is to bake from the rise we expect. If the dough climbs and clears the line, bake it, otherwise hold it. We set the line from the fuel. We use the poke test to read the dough and use it to decide the loaf size.

The idea is to build from the fit we expect. If the joint closes and clears the line, glue it, otherwise hold it. We set the line from the blades. We use the flex test to read the board and use it to decide the frame size.
Our way is to read the next rise closely and then bake by the "fold, then bake" rule. This is a plain, effective way to bake, above all when only the dough in front of us is known.
Our way is to read the next fit closely and then build by the "scribe, then glue" rule. This is a plain, effective way to build, above all when only the boards in front of us are known.

After the bake, the taste test, and the keeping test, we can say the following. The flour started as one bag and ended as a full rack. The amounts were tuned. The bake leans hard on the rye heat and far less on the wheat heat.

After the glue-up, the load test, and the season test, we can say the following. The timber started as one stack and ended as a full order. The sizes were tuned. The build leans hard on the pine depth and far less on the oak depth.
The above sums up our bake. We hope it gives you something you can use.
The above sums up our build. We hope it gives you something you can use.
The chart shows the spring of the practice batch, the trial batch, the held-back batch, and the whole clears the line we set.
The chart shows the fit of the practice stack, the trial stack, the held-back stack, and the whole clears the line we set.
